teaser.en: Purple-stained fingers give away anyone who has been eating water berries straight from the tree.

summary.en: *Mzambarau* is the water berry, a dense, leafy tree of moist and riverside forest with clusters of purple-black fruit. It feeds people, and it is one of the sawn-timber trees Digo carpenters know.

about.en: *Mzambarau* is a dense, leafy tree with drooping branchlets. Its glossy leaves grow in opposite pairs, and new growth flushes a striking purple-red before turning green. After flowering it carries heavy clusters of small, purple-black berries, like a wild cousin of the Java plum grown in gardens.

where.en: It grows in moist forest and along rivers and streams, where its roots can reach water, hence the English name water berry.

uses.en: The berries are eaten fresh. The wood is one of the local timber species known to Digo carpenters for sawing into planks, and the tree also gives poles. The bark provides tannin and a dye.

names.en: Pakia records the Digo name *mzambarau*, the same as the Swahili; ICRAF's handbook gives *muziahi*. Swahili also has *mzuari*. In English it is the water berry. *Mzambarau* is also the name of the Java plum (*Syzygium cumini*), a close relative.

reason.en: Java plum, same genus and same name
Guava, from the same myrtle family

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
